utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Russo, you're on your feet. May I take it that you will call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if the witness is still in the witness room, then we could ask Madam Usher not to rush too much so that I can read meanwhile a decision by the Chamber, at least the reasons for a decision. I would like to deliver the reasons, the Chamber's reasons for granting trial-related protective measures for Witness 86. On the 24th of June, 2008, the Prosecution filed a motion requesting that the Chamber order the trial-related protective measures of pseudonym and face and voice distortion for Witness 86. On the 25th of June, the Cermak Defence filed a response in which it did not oppose the request for protective measures. The Cermak Defence observed, however, that in order to prevent the identity of the witness becoming known, it is most likely that the testimony of the witness would be heard entirely in closed session. The following day, the Markac Defence filed its response not opposing the request for protective measures, though disagreeing with the Prosecution's arguments in support of the motion. Also on the 26th of June, 2008, the Gotovina Defence stated in court that it did not oppose the motion but similarly disagreed with the Prosecution arguments in support of the motion. The Gotovina Defence joined the observation of the Cermak Defence on the need to hear the testimony of the witness in closed session. These submissions of the Gotovina Defence can be found at transcript pages 5225 and 5226. At transcript page 5226, the Prosecution agreed with the Defence on the need to hear the testimony of Witness 86 in closed session. On the same day, the Chamber granted the motion and decided that in order to protect the identity of the witness it would hear the testimony of the witness in private session unless a party applied for a portion to be heard in public session. This decision can be found at transcript pages 5227 and 5228. The public was informed of this decision at transcript pages 5230 and 5231. The Chamber held in its reasons for its first protective measures decision in this case, which can be found on the pages 2610 and 2611, that the party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. This standard can be satisfied by showing, for example, that a threat was made against the witness or the witness's family. The mere expression of fears by a person is insufficient to justify protective measures. Witness 86 is a Serb who lives in Croatia. Following Operation Storm he continued his professional activities in Croatia. The Chamber found that the expected testimony of Witness 86 could antagonise certain persons in the place where he lives and works. The witness had already experienced, apparently as a result of media attention, that unidentified individuals attempted to contact him. In the absence of any objections raised by the Defence, the Chamber found, for the aforementioned reasons, that the Prosecution has demonstrated an objectively grounded risk to the security of Witness 86 should it become known that he has given evidence before the Tribunal. The Chamber furthermore considered that in light of the nature of the anticipated evidence of the witness, the only effective way to protect his identity was to hear his testimony in private session. And this concludes the Chamber's reasons for its decision to grant protective measures for Witness 86.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Dangerfield, at least I assume that you're Mr. Dangerfield. Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dangerfield. Please be seated. You will first be examined by Mr. Russo, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dangerfield. If you could please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: My full name is Mr. Roland Charles David Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, do you recall giving two statements to the ICTY, one dated the 21st of December, 1995, and the other dated 8 to 9 January 2008?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5263.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And Mr. Dangerfield, if I could direct you to the screen in front you. On the right-hand side, and I would ask Mr. Registrar to scroll, please, to the final page of that exhibit. Mr. Dangerfield, do you recognise this as the statement you gave the ICTY on 21 December 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5264. And again if we could scroll -- actually, I believe it will be to the third page of this particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, do you recognise this as the statement that you gave the ICTY on 8 to 9 January 2008?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, did you have a chance to review both of those statements prior to coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are both of those statements true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And do both of those statements accurately reflect what you told ICTY investigators?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions in court here today, would your answers be the same as in those two statements?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, they would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I move for the admission of 65 ters 5263 and 5264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 5263 becomes Exhibit number P695, and 65 ter 5264 becomes Exhibit number P696.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P695 and P696 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and if I could have the assistance of Madam Usher, would like to hand hard copies of the statements to the witness. And with the Court's permission, Your Honour, I'd like to read a brief summary of the 92 ter statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Roland Dangerfield was a sector liaison officer for the British contingent of the UNPROFOR mission and was based in Knin. Prior to Operation Storm, he travelled throughout Sector South to gather intelligence on HV and ARSK operations for Sector South commander General Forand. He observed that after an ARSK mobilisation on 27 July 1995, the town of Knin was virtually empty of any men of combat age and that there were no defensive positions or heavy weapons in the town. He was present in Knin during the artillery attacks on 4 and 5 August 1995, and observed the shelling the town approximately once an hour from the balcony of the UN HQ building. He heard rockets and heavy artillery fired into the town to begin attack on the morning of both days, which he described as intense and lasting for approximately an hour and a half on 4 August and half an hour on 5 August. He observed that after the initial salvo on each morning the shelling became sporadic and consisted only of heavy artillery. He also observed that no one area or military target ever appeared to be targeted by more than three or four rounds, and he described the artillery attack in general as a blanket shelling of Knin. He neither heard nor saw any outgoing fire from the town of Knin on the 4th or 5th of August, 1995. After Operation Storm, he witnessed HV soldiers looting houses in Knin while the police did nothing to stop it, but that houses marked with the phrase "Croatian house," in B/C/S were left alone. He travelled to Kistanje on 9 August 1995 where he found the town empty of civilians but houses burning and HV soldiers looting. He also travelled extensively throughout Sector South during August and September 1995 and recalled seeing Croatian special police preventing access to areas that were burning, and he estimated that approximately 80 to 90 per cent of the villages he saw suffered burning within the first few weeks after Operation Storm. Mr. President, Your Honours, that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, can you please tell the Court what your position and function was in Sector South in and around August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. In August 1995, I had been tasked by the British headquarters in Gornji Vakuf in Sector South-west to move to Knin, the headquarters of Sector South, to act as a liaison officer, and this was largely because there was a lack of information between the two sectors and it's customary on operations for sides to exchange liaison officers to establish what is going along -- on along the boundary between the two sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how far in advance of Operation Storm you began doing this?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I was there approximately six weeks to two months before Operation Storm began.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the court some idea of how much ground you covered in Sector South during that time?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Within Sector South I knew all the major routes. I travelled extensively with my driver off the main routes where there were barricades restricting my freedom of movement. I made sure it's my job to get round them and establish what was going on. And in short, I knew Sector South extremely well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did that include both the ARSK and the HV side of Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I made in my job to be on both sides of the border, because that was my job to establish what was going on on both the HV and the ARSK sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And you've mentioned roadblocks or restrictions on your movement. Can you give the court some idea of who restricted your movement and how?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you just repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Sure. You indicated in your previous answer that if there were roadblocks in your way you would try your best to get around them. I would like you to give the Court an idea for what kind of restrictions on your movement you faced.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Both sides, the HV and ARSK, typically put roadblocks up. This was barriers, rubble, sand, anything to restrict the movement across the roads. These were normally manned, and I was physically stopped from going through various areas, and that was by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And concentrating now just on the ARSK side of Sector South, can you give the Court any idea of where in general your movement was restricted?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: My movement was restricted particularly along the sensitive border areas. Within the actual centre of the sector it was not too bad. On occasion it was difficult, and on one occasion I was detained for two hours along with my driver, but I was released without any further action. So it was really restricted just along the sensitive border areas between the two warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did the ARSK also restrict your movement to inspect or observe ammunition or weapon sites?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The military and weapon sites were particularly sensitive, and therefore invariably I was not allowed to enter, and if at all possible, I was restricted from getting close to these sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And in spite of these restrictions, were you nevertheless able to get an impression for the relative capabilities of both the HV and the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If you can, please, can you tell the Court what your impression was of the capability of the ARSK to withstand an operation such as Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: When I travelled around Sector South, I was always surprised, I think it fair to say, how little heavy weaponry the ARSK had. Yes, they had tanks. Yes, they had artillery pieces. But I commanded a squadron of 12 Challenger tanks and I never in my whole travels around Sector South saw a collection of that many tanks in anyplace. So my assessment of the ARSK was they were woefully equipped to deal with any assault on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to move to a discussion of the situation in Knin in particular prior to Operation Storm, and if I could refer you to your first statement, that's the first tab you have there, your first statement at paragraph 23. And this is -- appears in e-court on the English on page 6, the B/C/S on page 4. Again at paragraph 23, you indicate that after the ARSK mobilisation on 27 July 1995, the town of Knin was virtually empty of any men of combat age. Can you please explain to the Court how it is you knew that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. In the six weeks to two months that I had been in Sector South and particularly in the Knin area, Knin was a busy town of its size, a lot of civilians, and indeed a largely -- no, that would be incorrect. A large amount of soldiers of combat age. And this was particularly on the day of rotation. Now, I can't specifically remember which day the rotation took place, but there was always a large number of soldiers in and around the bars and cafes of Knin. And this was apparent, because there seemed to be -- seemed to me to be far more military people than civilians within the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And after the mobilisation on the 27th of July?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: After the mobilisation on the 27th of July there were very few soldiers. In fact, I would take it down to a handful. And when I drove around Knin extensively to see what was left after the mobilisation, particularly around the military sites, I could put it down to possibly less than a hundred soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And moving to paragraph 15 of that same statement and in e-court the English this appears from pages 4 to 5, and in B/C/S it's on page 4. Now, Mr. Dangerfield, at paragraph 15 you indicate that on 29 July, civilians in Knin were packing up and leaving on buses along a route into Bosnia. And I would like you, please, to explain to the Court first again how you knew that and what exactly the information was you collected.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Within Knin town itself there appeared to be a large amount of the civilian population packing up, and they were leaving their houses carrying suitcases, plastic bags, and in fact I would describe it as their worldly possessions, and it was clear that they were leaving the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in that paragraph you reference a very specific route by which they left on buses. Can you tell the Court how you know that they took that route?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I was fascinated that so many people were leaving the area, and I made it my business to follow them and establish exactly what it was that they were doing, and so those buses I followed on the route that I described in my statement, and that is accompanied by specific grid references detailing that route.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Court any idea of whether this appeared to be officially organised or conducted according to some plan?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. With all due respect, that's if he knows and no speculation, please. If he doesn't know, he doesn't know. If he has information -- concrete information and not speculation, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo asked whether on its appearance the witness gained the impression that this was officially organised or -- organised or conducted according to a plan. And, Mr. Dangerfield, therefore you're invited to first describe your observations, and if that on the basis of that information you formed any opinion about it at the time - I'm not inviting you at this moment to develop further opinions on it - you may tell us, but please first describe what you observed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My observations were that the transport that the civilian population was getting into ranged from at one end the buses and trucks. In the middle of that ranged cars and any other such vehicles, and at the bottom end it would have been trailers towed by horses, donkeys, mules. And those were my specific observations. There was no marshalling areas for an exodus of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Dangerfield, did you see any ARSK military or police officials involved in this movement of people?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I assume, by just time-frame, I assume we're talking about the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Actually, we're talking about the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 29th of July. So be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was clear from the previous questions and, Mr. Kehoe, therefore, I think there was no need at this moment to intervene. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With all due respect, Judge, with a record that will be reviewed down the line, I just wanted to get a specificity on the date. I apologise for any inconvenience and I just wanted verify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's for the second time, now, that you now intervene between question and answer and that's, of course, what is certainly allowed to do if there is any need to do that but otherwise it might interrupt the flow of evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, I'd like to move now to the events of 4 August 1995, and if you could please describe for the court what you personally saw and heard of the artillery attack on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, are you interested in receiving an answer on the question you put to the witness before Mr. Kehoe intervened?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you don't have to apologise. You are putting the question. I take it that you are interested, as is the Chamber, to hear the answer. Perhaps you now repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, again confining yourself to what you personally observed and within the time-frame of 29 July 1995, can you please tell the Court whether you saw any RSK military or police officers involved in the movement of people out of Knin.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I saw no official police or ARSK soldiers involved in that movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. So now we'll move to the 4th of August, and again I'll ask you to please describe for the Court what you saw and heard of the shelling on that day.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: It was just before 5.00 in the morning, and I was up and about in the headquarters of Sector South. I was getting ready for the day's work, and shortly before 5.00 there was an incredible noise over and around the top of the UN headquarters. It was a massive noise. It sounded like a giant sheet of paper being ripped. There was a whoosh, a whoosh, whoosh, whoosh, and this initially I did not know what it was. However, it became very apparent quickly that we or the surrounding area was receiving a lost incoming rocket fire, and this was then accompanied by artillery fire, and the difference between the two is that the artillery shells have a whistling sound as they come in. At that stage, as you would understand, I was in an unprotected building. I decided that I'd had enough and along with my driver we grabbed all of our equipment and ran for the bunker. Now, the bunker is a bunker. It is not a soundproof building. And that fire of rockets and artillery continued approximately for the next 90 minutes continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Court what you witnessed when you emerged from this bunker and approximately at what time you actually came out of the bunker?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: From my recollection it was approximately 6.30 a.m. or just after. We came out of the bunker. There was still artillery screaming in but obviously not of the same intensity that it had been for the previous 90 minutes. It was the early morning, and Knin was covered in a blanket of dust and smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if I can -- well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: First let me ask you, after you emerged from the bunker did you at any time observe the town of Knin and where shells were falling?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Initially, it was very difficult to see where the shells were falling because of this blanket of smoke, and the UN headquarters, when you stand on the balcony there, was roughly at the same level as the smoke. So you could tell that it was the top. But the climatic factors prevailed. It was the summer, and as the temperature rose, so the ground heated up and the smoke -- the smoke dissipated, the dust settled, and from I, would put it, the middle of the morning you could start to see shells landing. You could continually hear them screaming into the town, and so you had -- or certainly I had a better idea of where they were landing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And let me refer you now to paragraph 30 of your first statement, and in e-court in the English that is page 7 to 8, and in B/C/S pages 5 to 6. Mr. Dangerfield, in paragraph 30 you indicate some areas where you saw shells landing on that day, and I'll ask you if you recall marking these areas on an aerial photograph of Knin.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5355.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if I may, I will simply walk you through some of these making reference to paragraph 30. In that paragraph you indicate that you saw shells landing in residential areas north of the Pol station, and I'll ask you if those areas are the two which you had marked as A on this picture.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mention you saw shells landing in the vicinity of the railway station, and I will ask you if that corresponds to the circle marked as B.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again you indicate shells fell near an ammo bunker 200 metres west of the UNHQ compound, and I'll ask you if that is the circle marked as C.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Again the parliament building, and I will ask you if that is the area marked as D.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The area you indicate where shells fell around the base of the Knin castle, is that the area which you have marked as E?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And the helipad or football pitch, is that the area marked as F?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And finally the Pol station, is that the area marked as G?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And to be clear, Mr. Dangerfield, are all of these areas where you personally observed shells landing?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would move for admission of 65 ter 5355.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I object, Judge. This -- apparently, there was a map that was submitted that is attached for the 21 December 1995 that I note here is referred to in paragraph 35, and then I note that this map is one of -- that was done here in 2008 to 22nd of July, 2008. I am frankly more interested in the one that was done 13 years ago. That's set forth in paragraph 35 as opposed to one that was done this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what was done when we do not know. We see that a date appears for the name of the witness, and the date is located this year. Mr. Russo, could you either, without giving evidence yourself, inform the Chamber, or could you clarify the issue together with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, could you please tell the Court when it was that you marked this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I marked this particular photograph on the date that I had signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can tell you we did receive a question from the Defence regarding the map which was originally attached to the statement. We indicated to the Defence that that map could not be found despite our efforts to locate it, which was in part the reason why I asked Mr. Dangerfield to again indicate these areas on the aerial photograph of Knin, and on that basis I would again move its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it is clear now that where the statement is from quite many years ago that the map was produced this same week. Any objections, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honours, not to admissibility but just to weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P697.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P697 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, if I could refer you to paragraph 26 of your first statement, and the e-court in English, this is at pages 6 to 7 and the B/C/S page 5. And if we could keep this image, please, up here on the screen. Mr. Dangerfield, I'm going to ask you a few questions about the military targets which you identify in paragraph 26, many of which are located next to or near the areas where you indicate you saw shells landing, and specifically looking at the two areas which you have marked as A on Exhibit P697, we can see that those two areas are on opposite sides of the Knin general supply which you have identified in paragraph 26 as a military target. One of the areas is directly north of the Pol station, as you also identify in paragraph 26, and the other is directly south of the main Knin army barracks, which you likewise identify as a military target in paragraph 26. I'd like you, if you can, to tell the Court based on what you observed whether the shells you saw landing in those two areas marked as A appear to have been fired at one of the military targets near them.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Within those areas initially there were a few rounds, but as the day went on, it became apparent to me that there were far too many shells landing in those areas to be dependent on ballistic variations in the rounds and indeed any associated climatic conditions that could cause them to fall there. So it was my assessment that there were indeed too many shells falling into those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And likewise for the area marked as B, it is clearly adjacent to the railway station in which you also identify as a military target. Does the same situation apply to the area marked as B?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And again the area that you mark here as E, around the base of the Knin castle, that is bordered again by things you identify as military targets. Does the same situation apply to the area marked as E?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I would give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could move to paragraph 32 of your statement, and the e-court in English is at page 8, in B/C/S it's page 6. In paragraph 32, Mr. Dangerfield, you indicate that refugees and troops began withdrawing through Knin at approximately 1700 hours and that the shelling at that stage was at a minimum. I would like you please to give the Court some idea of what this minimum was in terms of intensity or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: There had been the initial bombardment for the first 90 minutes of the day from 5.00. As I indicated earlier on, that intensity lessened, and it was sporadic artillery fire throughout the rest of the day. So when I say a minimum, it was that continued intensity. I would suggest, in my opinion, that a minimum is enough to be noticeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And did it appear to you that the troops and military vehicles which you indicate were part of this movement, did it appear to you as though they were guarding the retreat of the civilians who were also retreating?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The column of military vehicles and personnel and civilian personnel were leaving. There was no indication of any fighting withdrawal. There was no tank barrels pointing in the direction of the suspected HV threat, and that was of the minimal number of tanks that there were. So no -- there was no fighting withdrawal, and to me it was a rapid exodus and almost each for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You said that you would suggest that in your opinion a minimum is enough to be noticeable. Now, that, of course, requires an understanding of what you consider noticeable. If you say one shell an hour can be noticed and in that sense would be noticeable, then even one shell in 24 hours would be noticeable. So to be quite honest, I am a bit lost with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two to three rounds per minute, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If we could move briefly to your second statement. I believe that is P696. At paragraph 5 and e-court in English this appears at page 2, and likewise in the B/C/S. Mr. Dangerfield, in paragraph 5 there you indicate that at 1900 hours, the intensity of the shelling, it decreased significantly, but that there was a heavy volley of shells lasting approximately 15 minutes landing in the town on the night of 4 August. Are you able to tell the Court when, if at all, the shelling actually stopped on that night?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The shelling did not stop that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court what time you went to bed or what time you stopped observing this shelling?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: It was later on in the evening, sometime between the hours of 10.00 and 12.00 at night, and it was at that stage that I was going to go to bed. In fact, I was considering not going to the bunker at all. I considered the sporadic shelling that was continuing not to be a threat to the UN headquarters. But at approximately sometime between those two hours that intensity kicked up again, definitely with artillery shells and a few rockets, and it was at that stage that myself and my driver headed for the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the 4th of August, Mr. Dangerfield, were you sending reports on what was happening in Knin to the British G2 cell?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I could not for the first hour and a half because I was in the bunker, but once we came out at approximately 6.30 in the morning we were able to gather what reports there were from the various national battalions within the sector, and equipped with my satellite telephone I was able to file reports through to the British headquarters in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 446.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, do you recognise this document as one of the reports you prepared on 4 August?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I believe you've already touched on it a bit, but can you just give the Court an idea of where the information for this report comes from?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: This is the overview document, and therefore it is a summary constructed by me from the various reports that we received from the national battalions within the area known as Sector South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, on your exhibit list, under 446 we find different ERN numbers than the ones we find on this document. I'm not trying to make matters even more complex, because the numbers indicated there are following the numbers. If we look at the statements, apparently they have been either attached or having been very close to that, and now we have different numbers. I don't know whether there's -- is there any explanation for or is it just to be ignored? If so, you would be invited next time to give the ERN numbers you're using in court on your exhibits list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll certainly take your guidance on that. I can tell the Court that this particular document arrived in our office through several means. One, as you can tell, from General Andrew Leslie, which is why the AL5 appears at the top. It was attached to one of his statements. It also came to our office separately on its own and once again it was attached to the supplemental witness statement of Mr. Dangerfield, and each time it came in it received a different electronic reference number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I just hope that we have the right ERN numbers in the e-court version so that we're using the same here in court as -- because I do not know whether you uploaded the others ones or -- apparently, you uploaded this one but perhaps the others ones as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This one was the first -- uploaded the first we received that's why it made it on to the 65 ter list first, and I thought it would be, perhaps, duplicative to re-upload it as part of the supplemental statement. So simply I kept this one where it was and removed it from the supplemental statement when that was uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, of course, it remains a puzzle how the other number came to appear on your 65 ter list but let's forget about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the admission of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes exhibit number P698.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P698 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, moving now to the 5th of August, I would ask you again to very briefly explain for the Court your observations of the artillery attack on that day.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The artillery attack on the 5th of August started just again before 5.00 in the morning, and the initial intensity was of a similar level to that on the 4th of August. And that continued for approximately 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And where were you during this initial half an hour?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I -- I was again in the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what you did after you came out of the bunker?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: It was a similar process to the previous day. I made it my business to find out what was going on again throughout the area known as Sector South to establish exactly what the HV movement was and indeed any ARSK movement. And I filed my report through to the British headquarters as I had done on the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Referring back to paragraph 30 of your first statement, you indicate, I'll quote: "On both the morning of 04 and 05 August, there was so much artillery fire it could not possibly have been directed because there was so many shells and rockets landing in such a short time." If you're able I'd like you to explain to the Court exactly why you believe that the number of shells landing in a given area would have an impact on the ability to direct fire?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: As I explained there was a blanket of dust and smoke across Knin in those early hours, and that blanket was sufficient that even from our close vantage point you could not see exactly where those rounds were landing. Now, in order to adjust the fire and give it accuracy, you must see where it is landing, make your adjustments, and continue. And therefore, the weight and intensity of that fire almost prohibited these actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving now to paragraph 33 of that statement, and this appears in e-court at page 9 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S. You indicate, and I'll quote again: "From 10.45 hours you could hear the odd tank round and many small arms rounds being fired. There was no artillery, and I could neither hear or see any resistance." Can you please clarify for the Court whether this tank and small-arms fire that you heard was coming from inside Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The small-arms fire and tank fire was not coming from inside Knin. Indeed, throughout the entire time I was there I never saw or heard any fire going out from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you then tell the Court where the tank and small-arms fire was coming from at that time on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: From our position in the UN headquarters, judging by the sound, I would say it appeared to come from the area -- the settlement known as Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And is that to the south of Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: From recollection it's the south-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the sounds of tank and small-arms fire, did it sound to you like the sounds of combat?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: It did not sound like combat. Indeed there seemed to be no retaliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And later in that same paragraph you indicate that the 7 Puma Brigade was the first to enter Knin with their tanks and APCs arriving in a convoy, not moving tactically, which led you to believe that they did not expect any resistance, and I'd like you please to explain to the Court why tanks arriving in a convoy would indicate to you that no resistance was expected?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: From my experience of tanks, tanks moving along a road move tactically. It is not a safe area to be going along. They move along leapfrogging each other along the critical points of a road thus clearing the way ahead for troops following. These vehicles moved in a column, people on top of the tanks, in the vehicles, all together in one long column, cheering, and it was perfectly clear they were expecting no ARSK soldier or attack from within Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to the following paragraph. You indicate: "There seemed to be little control once the HV entered Knin. Troops systematically looted house. Small-arms fire and mysterious detonations were heard for at least a week afterwards." Can you tell the Court whether you personally observed these things happening?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously I had very little view on that initial day because I was confined to the UN barracks, but on the 7th of August, but more particularly the 9th of August, I was able to get out in my Land Rover with my driver and start patrolling again. There were HV soldiers in large numbers within Knin, and it was clear that there was little or no control. I saw soldiers going into and out of houses removing various electrical items and anything else that they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could please cabin you if you're able to recall specifically, you mentioned the 7th of August. Can you tell the Court, did you get out of the compound and into Knin on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. That was a particular day because it was the day that the UN special envoy Yasushi Akashi visited. I believe he landed in -- on the helicopter pad of the UN barracks and part of a long convoy including press. We escorted him to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And did you stay escorting Mr. Akashi around for the day?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I did not. As soon as we had a chance, on the way back myself and my driver broke away from that convoy and took a look and a patrol around Knin town, and therefore from a first-hand account of myself I was able to see exactly what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And on that day, the 7th of August, what exactly was going on?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: As I described earlier on, that was when the looting was going on. The general lack of discipline and control. It was clear to me that the soldiers were doing what they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you see any officers or commanders present while this was happening?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No. It was -- it was particularly evident that there were no officers or anyone who appeared to be in a position of authority controlling what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that you had gotten away from Mr. Akashi's convoy. And if someone had been off of that convoy, would what you saw have been evident to anyone not following that column?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. This was completely overt behaviour, and even when we drove past it did not stop, and it seemed to be the normal behaviour throughout the town on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Later in that same paragraph you say that: "Trucks pulled up at houses. I witnessed all sorts of electrical items being loaded into cars by soldiers while police did nothing to stop it. This went on for at least two weeks." I'd like you to please clarify for the Court whether this particular sentence refers to events that you witnessed happening in Knin.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: As soon as I got an opportunity to patrol out of Knin, I made it my business, as I had done prior to the 4th of August, to patrol throughout Sector South. And on -- or, rather, in those areas that I patrolled, that behaviour seemed to be the pattern throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And based on your own observations, did this kind of looting continue in Knin for two weeks after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. At least two weeks, I would say, and it was throughout Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The trucks -- trucks and cars being used during this looting, can you tell the Court whether these were military trucks or civilians?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The vehicles being used were both military and civilian. It appeared to me that whatever vehicle you had, you filled it up with whatever you could get your hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, is there any doubt in your mind as to whether the individuals you saw engaged in this behaviour were in fact HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Does he have some background information? That's pure speculation. Has he any doubt? What is replete in this is that people in camouflage uniforms, as the Prosecution well knows the entire place had camouflage uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was not whether they were soldiers or not but whether the witness had any doubt on his mind but if it ever came up. That is, of course -- that was the question, but before that question be put to the witness I think we, Mr. Russo, you should go in some detail as to what he described as far as the appearance of the persons he saw taking whatever they wanted. And I think at an earlier stage the witness testified that these were military, but I have to find that and see whether that's correct. At the same time, I remember from his statement that he refers to how people were dressed or sometimes about military and civilians. Could you please, before you ask him whether -- and that is a question of fact, whether ever doubt came to his mind. If you ask me whether I ever doubted some matters, that is just a matter of fact. But before you put that question, of course, it would be good to see what observations created an apparent impression and what circumstances perhaps may have caused any doubt on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I may, Judge, what this Court has said over and over again is that the Court and the Chamber wants facts. Not speculation, just facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, I said that the question of whether I ever experienced doubt on my mind is a question of fact. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand your interpretation, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo, nevertheless you're invited to first explore what the witness observed and what at any time would or would not have created either an impression in his mind or doubt on his mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, you indicated at the inception of your testimony that prior to Operation Storm you had had the opportunity to visit both sides, both HV and ARSK sides of the zone of separation. Let me ask you first, while you were on the HV side did you have an opportunity to see what kinds of uniforms the HV soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I knew the difference between ARSK soldiers and HV soldiers when wearing their uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can you give the Court a description of the typical -- or what HV soldiers' uniforms looked like?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I'm afraid after 13 years my memory on that is not distinct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Did you at the time, when you were on the HV side of the zone of separation, have an opportunity to see the kinds of trucks and vehicles which were used by the HV army?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- I object at this point. We're now in 2008 with the witness giving testimony, and he doesn't recall, and to try to bootstrap our way into this by something back in 1995, I object. He doesn't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the first question what he didn't recall was about how people were dressed, and I think this question is now about trucks and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then what I caution the Chamber is that that's the road that the Prosecution is trying to travel on, and I just bring this up as a cautionary measures and we'll see where the questioning goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: If I could -- do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No. I think I can make it a short answer. On those days that I was travelling within Knin and throughout Sector South, when I saw the looting the large numbers of individuals carrying out that looting were wearing HV uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Let me take you back to the previous question. When you were on the HV side of the zone of separation prior to Operation Storm, did you have an opportunity to observe the vehicles that the HV were using?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and prior to my deployment to the area part of my training had been specific recognition of the warring factions' vehicles, uniforms, ranks, and insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the vehicles that were used in the looting after Operation Storm, which you indicate in paragraph 34, were used during this looting, were those the same kinds of vehicles you saw on the HV side of the zone separation?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, they were, and invariably their registration plates had the letters HV, Hotel Victor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And I understand that you have difficulty recollecting here and now. I'll ask you, when you made your first statement in December of 1995 and indicated that there were soldiers doing certain things, at that time did you have a clear recollection of what, for example, HV soldiers wore?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 13 of your first statement, in e-court this appears page 4 of English and page 3 of the B/C/S, in paragraph 13, Mr. Dangerfield, you indicate that there were houses that were spared from looting and that these had signs on them. I would like you to please explain that for the Court.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. In short, those houses had in Serbo-Croat the words "Croatian house," and that was painted on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: How did you know that they said "Croatian house"?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Again I, as the British Army always does, received basic training in the language of the country that we would be visiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And is your command of the Serbo-Croat language the same today?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is an appropriate time for a recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We started at a quarter past 2.00. The first session usually takes one hour and a half. So there is still 15 minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, you indicate at paragraph 9 of your first statement, this appears in English at pages 3 to 4 and in B/C/S at page 3, in paragraph 9 you indicate that the first time you got out of the compound you witnessed the "complete change to Knin." I would like you to please explain to the Court what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The complete change to Knin applied to the population and the state of the city. As I indicated earlier on, it had been a -- what I would describe as a bustling town for its size. People frequenting the bars and cafes, going about their everyday business. After the 4th and 5th of August, it became clear to me that there were very few civilian personnel remaining within that city. The population had diminished, and indeed when I travelled around the city I saw evidence of the considerable bombardment that that city had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Can I take that last sentence of your answer -- well, let me just ask you. Did you observe shelling damage in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and it was clear that it was fresh shelling damage, and again we had received training in identifying from which directions mortars and shells, by their distinctive patterns had come. It was also clear to me that the buildings in the areas that I described and highlighted on the map had also been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And are you referring to the areas which you circled on the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I am indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether the damage that you saw from shelling was concentrated or confined to any particular areas of the town?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: It was throughout the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to discuss your observations of what happened outside of Knin in the weeks following Operation Storm. In paragraph 10 of your first statement, and in e-court that is page 4 in English and page 3 in B/C/S, in paragraph 10, Mr. Dangerfield, you indicate that on 9 August, which was the first time that you had a patrol, you visited the town of Kistanje, and can you please describe to the Court what it was you witnessed happening in that town.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I remember it well. When we drove into the outskirts of Kistanje it was clear to me that there were a lot of individuals dressed in Croatian military uniform. The atmosphere was tense. My appearance in the Land Rover that I was travelling was clearly unwanted. The other thing that was particularly noticeable to me, that there seemed to be a lack of artillery or indeed fire from tanks. There was -- i.e., there was no damage to the buildings from that sort of thing, and that was recognisable. What was clear was that the vast majority of Kistanje was on fire. Soldiers were there doing looting, celebratory fire into the air, and indeed there was -- appeared to be a complete lack of control of what was going on in Kistanje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you give the Court some idea of approximately how many Croatian soldiers you saw in the town?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: From my judgement it was company strength. So I think we would be looking at approximately 150 to 200 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And again were you able to distinguish any officers or commanders in that town?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No. It was the same story as it had been throughout the rest of the sector on my patrols. There just seemed to be an apparent lack of control over what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Were there any civilians present in Kistanje on that day?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: On that day I saw no civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, did you travel to other towns and villages within Sector South in the weeks following Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And again if you could give the Court some idea of the amount of ground you covered within Sector South in those weeks?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Within those weeks, as I had done prior to the 4th and 5th of August, I travelled extensively throughout Sector South. Indeed, I remember surviving on six hours sleep a night, travelling and patrolling for at least another 14 hours throughout the day, and with the remaining time I had I was writing and filing my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in your second statement, which I believe is P696, at paragraph 7 -- this is e-court English page 2, as well as the B/C/S. In that paragraph, Mr. Dangerfield, you estimate that 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the villages that you saw in Sector South in the weeks after Operation Storm suffered some form of burning. Can you tell the Court whether that estimate is based on your personal observations?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: It is indeed, and that percentage I would describe as extremely accurate, and it appeared that the majority of the sector was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: In the next paragraph on -- in that statement you indicate that you personally observed HV soldiers standing around in towns and villages where houses and crops were burning. Can you give the Court any idea of how often you saw this type of thing?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: This was a daily occurrence. In fact, one almost became blase about it. You travelled around the area and it was just a familiar picture and sight on every day. On one occasion I visited the village of Cetina and this standard behaviour of looting and burning was going on. In fact, for a while my presence was not noticed, and indeed a truckload of soldiers drove into the village all firing their weapons into the air. When our presence was noticed, we were detained. Momentarily admittedly. Identification was checked, and I would say it was for no longer than five or ten minutes, but nevertheless we were detained, and after some discussion we were escorted from the sector and indeed made it our business to find a route back into the sector to continue with our routine patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: When you say escorted out of the sector, does that mean out of Sector South entirely?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And staying in that same paragraph, Mr. Dangerfield, you indicate that Croatian special police prevented access to areas that were burning. And I'd like you to please tell the Court whether you were ever personally prevented by the special police from entering areas that were burning.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And at the time did you know what a special police officer was, and can you tell the Court how you knew that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I had received the training prior to deployment, and we knew the order of battle of all the military and what I would describe loosely as paramilitary personnel. Not just on the Croatian side but on the Bosnian side and the Serbian side, and that was standard practice for our training.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dangerfield, do you recall writing an article regarding your experiences during and after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar if we could have 65 ter 5265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, are you referring to the essay "The Fall of the Republic."

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I do understand there is an objection to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know if whether there's an objection. It's not on the 65 ter list, isn't it? There is first an application to have it on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against having it added to the 65 ter list which is not yet the same as being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. And my objection with regard to this document was not through Major Dangerfield but through another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but -- first thing first. There's no objection against adding it to the 65 ter list. Mr. Russo, therefore that request is now granted. Please proceed, and if it comes to tendering the document, we'll hear from the Defence whether in relation to this witness there will be any objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at the same time I'm looking at the clock. I don't know how much time you'd still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I was going to admit this document and complete my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we'd better finish. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, looking at the document on the screen, is this the article that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court when it was written?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. It was constructed from my reports gathered over the period, but I constructed this particular document ten days after the 4th and 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would move for the admission of 65 ter 5265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a contemporaneous document drafted by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objections, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number P699, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P699 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes my examination. And thank you, Mr. Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Russo. Since you've got one minute left before the break, I would seek on one point clarification. Mr. Dangerfield, when you were invited to describe the sound of combat, you used the word "retaliation," which in law has a very specific meaning, and I wondered whether in more neutral terms you were referring to what I learn to be return fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be correct. I heard no return fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're standing, so I inform Mr. Dangerfield that you'll now be cross-examined, Mr. Dangerfield, by Mr. Kehoe who is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, you noted during the course of your direct examination that you were filing continuous reports over the course of the 4th and the 5th and I suppose thereafter, and we have been presented with your report P697 of the 4th of August, and this is a one -- three-page report. Are there others?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Not in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what does that mean, "not in existence"? Where are they? Or what happened to them, better still?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: They would have been filed along and kept for record by my headquarters. When I say "my headquarters," I say the Sector South-west British headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And when you say that they are no longer in existence, what did your British headquarters in Sector South do with a UN document?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I have no idea. When I say "not in existence," I was referring -- what I actually meant is I have none of them in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So as far as you know, these reports should still be with the UN?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: If that is what they have chosen to do is to keep them, then yes. If they haven't, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dangerfield, do you know if for a fact your reports were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you mentioned to us that they were no longer in existence, did someone tell you that they had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you sent these reports to your headquarters in Gornji Vakuf; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also sent them to your British headquarters in Split, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, do they exist at the British headquarters in Split?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do your reports still exist that you sent to the British headquarters in Split?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That headquarters ceased to exist some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if I may ask your attention for the question, which was slightly differently phrased the second round. First Mr. Kehoe asked whether they exist at the British headquarters in Split, but when he repeated his question, "Do your reports still exist that you sent to the British headquarters in Split?" which is different because they may be somewhere else but he was now identifying your reports by the ones being sent to Split, so therefore whether those headquarters still do exist is not relevant. It's the existence of the reports sent to that headquarters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying the question, sir. I don't know whether those reports still exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, where were the records that were at British headquarters in Split be archived?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I do not know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you also sent your records to the Ministry of Defence in London, too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did you seen them to London?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I did the.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the only two locations you're saying that you went them were to -- were the British headquarters in Gornji Vakuf and the British headquarters in Split.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it's important to clarify that whilst every report should have gone to the headquarters in Gornji Vakuf, it was on my own decision-making process as to whether they should go to the headquarters in Split. So I don't believe that every report will have gone to the headquarters in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who is DLC in your distribution network in P697?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I believe those letters stand for data link cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what is a data link cell?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You have no idea?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that may be part of the headquarters that collate the material that I sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: But apart from that, I cannot be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, you were sending it to Split. You were sending it to Gornji Vakuf, and you're sending it to this DLC, but you don't know what DLC is?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I know what the letters stand for, but the exact make-up of that particular organisation I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, when -- when the information was going to DLC, who was on the receiving end of that information?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't know. As a military man, occasionally or more often than not you are given orders, and you carry out those orders to the best of your ability. Sometimes that means that you do things that not all the time you know why, and not always is it the case is it my position to question why. It is my position to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, who gave you the order to send these reports to DLC?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: It would have been my chief sector liaison officer in the headquarters in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That would have been Major -- Major May of the Royal Marines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what is Major May's first name, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't know his first name, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But he was a Royal Marine?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you -- was the recipient of this information on DLC, was that MI6?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, were you working for MI6 at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if you were working for MI6, would you know?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So what you're saying is when you were operating in the field, you could have been working as a representative or agent of MI6, right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you just told us that were you working for MI6, and you said, "As far as I know, no." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And then I asked you, "If you were working for MI6, would you know?" And your answer was, "I don't think so."

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. As you moved around the area, you were trying to gather information on HV movements and ARSK movements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the reason why you were sent by your headquarters in Gornji Vakuf to Knin was to gather yet more information. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I can turn your attention to your reports, and I am referring to your reports now, and I'm talking about P698, and if I may be mistaken I may have these numbers incorrect, Madam Registrar, but I do believe that P698 was the last document that -- that the witness put in, which is The Fall of the Republic of Serb Krajina. I believe -- is that's 697, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was 699, but correct me when I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: 699. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you note that in the beginning of -- this is in paragraph 2 of 699, if we could bring that up, "Since May of this year our job had been to monitor the build-up of Croatian forces to the western cell in south-east of the United Nations sector. We also had been monitoring the response to this by the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina." Now, you knew, sir, when you came -- let me withdraw that and backtrack a bit. Before you went to Knin, you knew that the HV troops that were in the Livno Valley and up on the Dinara were commanded by General Gotovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you did receive information about HV movements going up the Livanjsko Polje valley prior to the attack on Grahovo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: To clarify, receiving information, I would have been informed about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, prior to going into Knin you did receive briefings and other items of information in your headquarters in Gornji Vakuf as to what was going on in the Krajina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I remember receiving a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that was so you could better understand what was going on when you eventually got to Knin. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think that's fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us go to an exhibit and if we can do our best to recreate this briefing, and if I may get this number correctly, and that is 1D420015. And, Mr. Dangerfield, this is series of slides that I'd like to take you through.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dangerfield, these are a series of military operations by the HV forces beginning in the winter of 1994 and culminating in the fall of 1995, and approximately the 11th of October. And if we can go through the next slide.
