Now, just to orient you on this, as you can see it's the HVO ABiH held territory and of course the other areas of Bosnia and Croatia with the Bihac pocket in the centre. And throughout your time there there were attacks on and off on the Bihac pocket by the Serb forces, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I was not monitoring Bihac, so I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you were in G2 we know from your statement, and G2 is an intelligence gathering component, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I would say information gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll use your word. It's an information gathering component. And when you were getting your debriefing as to what was going on with the HV, it's fair to say that as part of giving you a view of the terrain, you were told what the situation was in the area in 1994 and 1995, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: You said I was getting a debriefing. I never received a debriefing. My job was to concentrate on the area known as Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you did receive a briefing, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be debriefing, briefing apparently is the issue, Mr. Kehoe. I heard something which sounded to me as briefing but is on the transcript as debriefing. I'm referring you to page 46, line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Maybe I'll withdraw. Maybe we're talking past each other just a tad, Your Honour, and I'll clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you told us you received training in languages. You received training in military. You used training on the warring factions, and you received training on uniforms. Did you also receive training on weapon systems?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: When you say "training on weapon systems," could you clarify exactly what you mean, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you given information by your headquarters on weapon systems?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Recognition of weapon systems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You were given training on recognition of weapon systems in addition to the other items of training I just talked about, that being language, uniforms, the warring factions. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as part of the information you received, let us turn to the next slide. This is Operation Winter '94, 29 November to 24 December, 1994. Now, when you received the briefing, you also received information on the deployment of forces both on the HV side, and let me include HV-HVO side, as well as on the Serb side, and in that I mean the RSK side as well as the VRS, right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I'd just like to make a comment on these slides. These are not my slides. They are not the slides I would have been briefed with, if indeed I was briefed with slides at that time. Computer technology was not sufficient, nor was the funding within the British Army to produce such material. Therefore, I don't feel that I can comment on the slides that you are producing in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, I wish I had the slides or the information that you looked at when you were being briefed, but looking at the slide that is before you and looking at the information that you received by your headquarters in Gornji Vakuf, did they explain to you the operation run by the HV and the HVO under the command of General Gotovina in the winter of '95 and that the area -- excuse me, the winter of '94-'95, apologises -- excuse me, winter '94, or the area in blue was an area that was taken by HV-HVO forces during the time-frame 29 November to 24 December 1994?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think we had a rough idea of what was described as the zone of separation between the warring factions. What I think is clear is that they did not have sufficient detail, and therefore that is why I was deployed as the sector liaison officer between the sectors known as Sector South and Sector South-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, based on the information that you got at the time and the information that you received subsequently, do you look at this map and recognise that one of the first offensives in this series of offensives that was conducted by General Gotovina was Winter '94, and it took control of this area, as we move up the Dinara that is shaded here in the light blue?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: This was prior to my deployment, so I don't recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you received -- when you got a briefing, you received information about what was going on in the theatre prior to you getting to the theatre, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: We -- we got a strategic outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And part of that strategic outline included this military operation by the HV and the HVO in the winter of '94, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I do not recall this specific military operation being briefed. That's not to say I did not be briefed on it or was not briefed on it. I do not recall being briefed on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, were you briefed -- and my apologies, Your Honour if, I'm going too fast. Mr. Dangerfield, sometimes with us speaking the same language we need to just pause a bit. Were you briefed on these military operations in -- of any kind in the winter of 1994?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't believe I was briefed on specific military operations. I believe that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- Mr. Dangerfield, I now and then switch to other languages, and I have to check whether the translation is -- is where we are. That is what caused for a little bit of a longer pause. Mr. Kehoe, if you apologise for going too fast, ask someone to listen to the French or the B/C/S channel and find out whether they have finished their translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will give that task to Mr. Akhavan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. He's trained in languages as well. Yes, I do understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think the last -- because -- Mr. Kehoe, I have a bit of a problem. You produce on the screen an enormous lot of information, and I think the first thing, and it -- slowly we came to that, is to find out whether the witness was briefed about the operation Winter, and that could be asked even without having a lot of military information on a map which may be known, may be totally unknown to the witness. Therefore, let's go from the broad picture to the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Without talking about a specific operation, Mr. Dangerfield, were you briefed on what was happening up on -- in this area and up on the Dinara in the conflict that took place in the winter of '94? Do you recall that at all?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't have been briefed on such a specific operation. I would have been briefed on the rough outline of where the warring factions were, because of course when I deployed to the region, I was not initially deployed into this area. So my first job was doing something else as another sector liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, sir. Let me briefly go through, then, in your statement, and again I'm looking at P699. I don't know if you have that in front of you, Mr. Dangerfield, but --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Could you direct me more specifically, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the one, The Fall of the Republic of Krajina, the article that you wrote.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in the second-to-last paragraph in the second sentence -- pardon me, the third sentence, "Since May." Do you see that? "Since May the Croat forces"?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: "Since May of this year our job had been to monitor the build-up of Croatian forces," is that the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, sir. It's the one the -- the paragraph beginning "Around the 21st of July..."

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Okay. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now just go down to the third sentence.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, since -- it notes that since May the Croat forces had been attacking up the Livanjsko Polje valley to the east of the strategically important Dinara Mountains. So you did have briefings on the HV movement in the spring of 1995, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I -- I didn't have briefings. As I said, I received a briefing, and what I've written here will have been information that I made it my job to find out prior to my deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So you did learn that in fact there were HV offensives in the spring of 1995 up on the Dinara. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think I would have learned that the HV were gaining ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And let us look again -- and by the way, by this point when you were making it your business to find out what was going on, by this point in your job with G2 you knew that these HV forces were being commanded by General Gotovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I did know that, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us look at these next several slides quickly, and if is -- if we can go back to 1D420015. And if we could go to the third slide in. And I'm -- Mr. Dangerfield, I'm going to show you a couple of slides and then ask you a few questions. If you could go to the next slide. This is a depiction of the map immediately before Jump-1. Can we go to the next slide. If we can just look at that. This is the Jump-1 from 7 April 1995. The light blue area again being the area that was taken in Jump-1. If we go to the next slide. This is Jump-2. Now, this Jump-2, sir, takes place in June 4 to 11 of 1995. Now, in June you knew, sir, that there were attacks by the VRS in Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, and also additional pressure being put on Bihac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next slide which is the Jump-2 slide. Now, this is the -- again, sir, these are the operations. When you talk about your Croatian forces since May attacking up the Livanjsko Polje Valley, these are the operations that you're generally referring to; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think before I continue it's important to divorce my answer from the slides. I am answering the questions on my information that I've written here. So the information I will give you refers to this: I do not recognise these slides. There is a lot of small information on it which I haven't put there. It's not British. It hasn't been verified by me, so I cannot comment on anything of that. So when I write about something in here, it's a -- more strategic, it's an overview. It's the sort of information that you could read in a newspaper written by a defence correspondent. It is of no more detail than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, when you were providing information to your headquarters in Split and your headquarters in Gornji Vakuf and to DLC, whoever that is, you weren't providing them with information that they could run on -- read in the Daily Telegraph, were you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was important for them to know, consistent with what you said in your statement of P699, that your job -- or "Our job had been to monitor the build-up of Croatian forces."

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Just a word on the statements you refer to P699.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is the magazine article, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Okay. My paperwork is not labelled as such, so could we make sure we clarify exactly which statement it is when we speak about it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Absolutely. And --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- that's a fair comment, sir. And if at any time, Mr. Dangerfield, you have about what I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- please stop me.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if I overlook it, I will certainly provide it to you. What I was referring to just then was your article The Fall of the Republic of Serb Krajina, and that's P699. And frankly, when I give the designation P699, it's more for the record than it is for you. My question, if we can go back to that, is that the information that you were providing to your headquarters both in Gornji Vakuf and Split and to this DLC was information that was important for them to understand the Croatian -- the build-up of Croatian forces and the Croatian forces' activities; right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think it's important to note was not just Croatian. It was ARSK and all the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But talking about this particular operation in the spring -- in June of 1995 and the HV forces in this regard, this is the type of information you would be passing on to your headquarters and to DLC?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't comment on June of 1995. What I can comment on is the information on that particular operation in 1995, but what I can comment on is the information that is in the statements that I have given and any factual information that I got from off the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just waiting for my signal to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe, I earlier asked you to start with the broad picture. Did you ever report about an operation you knew under the name "Jump-2"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever report on an operation in which apparently combat took place close to the Croatian-Bosnian border between the 4th of June and the 11th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, what operations did you report on that you refer to in your article in the second to last paragraph of Croatian forces attacking up the Livanjsko Polje valley?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Okay. That information is information that I will have gained from general knowledge. As I said, the sort of information that you could gain from a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you report on the battle to take -- let me withdraw here, that you note again in your statement 699, that Bosanski --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the article again --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The article, my apologies, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because it confuses the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My apologies, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The article again in that same paragraph that: "Bosanski Grahovo was of vital for instance the Serb Krajina as it was their main supply route from the Bosnian Serb stronghold of Banja Luka." If we could turn to the next slide. Now, did you report on the fighting or the attack by the HV and the HVO on Bosanski Grahovo that you refer to in your Article P699?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I cannot remember specifically. If it's somewhere in any of my statements, could you please direct me to it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you talk about it, sir --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I talk about it in this article. If I have reported it somewhere else, could you direct me to it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, sir, I don't have the rest of your reports.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that is why I'm asking the question did you report on it. I note in your article P699, in the last two paragraphs you talk about the importance -- the vital importance of Bosanski Grahovo and in the next paragraph, "In the last week of July," and I'm quoting, "In the last week of July the Croat forces moved swiftly and decisively to take the town of Bosanski Grahovo. This was major blow to the Krajina Serbs as it cut off their supply route." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, in your question you said, "Did you" -- it says -- "All right. Under fighting or the attack by the HV and the HVO on Bosanski Grahovo that you referred to in your article P699." Now, the witness is asking where in this article he refers to the fighting or the attack by the HV and the HVO on Bosanski Grahovo. Where do we find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As I was just quoting, Your Honour, it is at the bottom of the first page on P699, and we can bring P699 back up on the screen, and we can see it in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it should be the bottom of page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that now clear to you, Mr. Dangerfield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You write about it, now Mr. Kehoe asks questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can go back to the 1D420015, the slide for Operation Summer '95. And then as that's coming up, Mr. Dangerfield, I refer you to your -- again, your article at P699, and you -- you note that in the first sentence in about the second week of July the Bosnian Serb army had attacked the UN declared safe area of Srebrenica and taken it. Now, if we can look at -- we can go to the next page of the slide -- excuse me, the preceding page, please. It should be -- that's right. That's fine. Now, if we see in the right-hand side of this photograph, as we move into July this is when the attacks were taking place on Srebrenica and Zepa. Excuse me, summer -- I'm sorry. It should be two prior to this slide, page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I'm -- the first sentence in about the second week of July, what page are we now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're still on page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still on page 1. Paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Staying with this, Mr. Dangerfield, this is the area, of the time-frame in July of 1995 where Srebrenica had been overrun, Zepa, there was attacks on Sarajevo, and also the Bihac pocket was being attacked by a combination of VRS and the ARSK along with the forces of Fikret Abdic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't recall specifically who was in charge of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if we move to the next page -- the next slide, excuse me. Just in the interest of time if we could go through this just briefly. This is the area, if you recall, that was taken by HV-HVO forces, including Grahovo, that you refer to in the last paragraph of P699. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: You're linking the slide to my statement. I have a to divorce both of them from each other. I do not know, and I don't recognise whether that is the correct line or not. So I can only comment on what is in my statement, and that is, as I said before, the sort of information that you or I could read in a newspaper written broad-brush by a defence correspondent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, is this the general a that was based on your recollection? Is this is the general area that had been taken by the HV-HVO in the Summer '95 operation?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I'm simply not prepared to comment on that because as I say I cannot comment on something that is not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us move to the next slide which is Operation Storm, and you did report on Operation Storm. If you could go to the next slide. Operation Storm we have this areas that are outlined, and if we can go to the next slide. Now, sir, you understood the importance of Operation Storm for the -- both the RSK and for the HV to take. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I was a 25-year-old captain when this happened, and you would have read this article, and to me the whole thing was very interesting. I was more interested on what was happening on the there and now, what was happening on me -- on my patrols. I may have understood the reasons why, but I was not working at the strategic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, you were there to gather information and to pass it on. When you were gathering this information, did you ask the questions as to why it was necessary for the HV, under the command of General Gotovina, to take Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I didn't ask the questions, but I think I probably knew it from background reading from books I probably bought in a library.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what did you know?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think Knin being a city, being probably the largest city -- or certainly it was the largest city within the area known as Sector South. I knew it was of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. And it was their communication centre, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was the ARSK centre of government, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you familiar at the time of any of the particular troop movements in and around Knin at the time? I'm talking about on the 4th and the 5th during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: On the 4th and the 5th we were in the barracks in the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you'd just go to the next slide quickly and we'll get through this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, that's not an answer to the question. The question was whether you were familiar at the time. That could have been by personal observation. That could have been by receiving information from other people. Even if you are, as you said, in the barracks, that doesn't necessarily mean that you do not become familiar with certain matters. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm just going to try to go through these and see exactly what you know, sir. This is the 8th of August, and are you familiar at the top of this item of the area where the confrontation -- confrontation line solidified as of the -- as of August 8th?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: This is a large-scale map. I dealt with maps 1:50.000 which to you and I means one square, one kilometre. That was the level of detail I was dealing with. So I can't comment on maps of this scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did the line -- if you look at the top, did the HV-VRS-ARSK line solidify itself in and around Drvar, and did you see that when you were driving around on the night?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't recall visiting specific places on specific dates. If you could direct me in my -- in my reports where that is, then maybe I can read it and look in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just taking you based on your statement that you were driving all around the place with your driver and your vehicle as of the 9th, and I'm asking you whether or not you saw this particular confrontation line or visited it.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't comment on the 9th, on specific dates, without my memory being jogged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next slide. Were you aware of a counter-strike by the -- by the -- excuse me, by the combined VRS-RSK forces? And if we can go -- on the 12th. And if we go to the next slide. And the counter-attack by HV forces under the command of General Gotovina on the 13th. Were you aware of that when you were down in the area?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't comment on the specifics of the map where it is indicated -- I believe you are indicating to whatever it is that took place. So I cannot comment further, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking without -- without -- if we can just move away from the specifics and just talk generally, were you aware of this going on on the 12th and the 13th of August?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I might have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you say you can't comment, does that mean you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't think it means I don't know. I just don't recall it. I just don't recall having information on it. I -- if it's -- I need to -- if you're asking me to comment on stuff, information that I've written in any of my reports that are present here, then, yes, I can, but I can't tie specific dates, places, actions, unless I've written on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean on that score let me just show you another map on the 18th of ground taken from the counter-attack of the HV forces under the command of General Gotovina. That would be the next slide. That shows the confrontation line as of the 18th after the counter-attacks. Now, just generally speaking on this entire matter, sir, you did know -- when did you leave Knin?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think it would have been early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So -- and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In early September, I mean, did you learn of the HV moving forward in early September in an operation called Operation Maestral? And let me just move to the next slide and let me put you in there. We can go to the next page. Now, you did know, Mr. Dangerfield, that the combined forces of the HV-HVO, along with the ABiH, did in fact attack the Bosnian Serb forces in conjunction with the ARSK, and did you learn that they took during this operation called Maestral from the 8th to the 15th of September, 1995, did you learn they took 2.500 square kilometres of territory and penetrated 30 kilometres into VRS territory? Did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: In September 1995 I was more interested in going home to England where I hadn't lived for five years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Dangerfield, the question was not what you were mainly interested in, but Mr. Kehoe put to you, I must say, quite a complex question containing a lot of information, so let's try to take it one by one. Did you know that the combined forces of the HV and the HVO, along with the ABiH, did attack the Bosnian Serb forces in early September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then I may take it that you didn't know that it was 2.500 square kilometres, that it was the 30 kilometres? It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier consulted my colleagues, and we all agreed that the purpose of hearing the testimony of a witness is not to educate the witness on the events that happened so that he goes home as a wiser man but that the Chamber hears evidence and that the Chamber learns more about what happened and what the witness can tell us. That might be a little bit lost in the last half hour, if not 35 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I will move ahead, and just given the witness's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I take it from your testimony that you have no further knowledge of HV activities after your departure in September of 1995. Is that accurate in?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we just move through the rest of these slides quickly. After Maestral I will show the Court these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this about what the witness just said, that he doesn't know anything about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, it's just that this is presenting the balance of this to the Chamber, and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are here to -- let's look at the next slide as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can -- I can deal with this after the witness gets off the stand with this particular document, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But have you really -- of course I wondered over the last half hour also whether a lot of these matters as to which party took control of what area, and even with the size of the areas, if the witness apparently and repeatedly told us that he does not have the oversight over what happened there, why not try to seek an agreement, because it seems that most of this most likely would not very much be contested when -- whether Bihac was in danger. I think we heard already some evidence on that. We have heard evidence on the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde. The witness clearly indicates that he was focusing on other matters. He learned from it as a newspaper reader on some elements. Why then not try to seek an agreement rather than spending 40 minutes in court on matters the witness says, "I was not focusing on that. I didn't know anything about that," where these seem to be issues that might not be that much contested? I take it there will not be much of a disagreement about who attacked Srebrenica, when it was attacked, what the status of Srebrenica was at that time. Similar issues for Bihac on which we heard some evidence as well. And now you are telling us, Mr. Kehoe, that you take us quickly through the remaining slides which contains, apparently, a lot of information which -- the basis for which is entirely unclear, maybe all through who was where, at what moment in time, what operation was running, but that's not the way this Chamber wants to receive evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I mean, just on the basis of how -- of going forward. It was the basis of providing and allowing -- putting -- we are required under the rules to put our case to the witness and if the witness doesn't know all this stuff that's fine. The fact is that if he does know something that's going to add to this, it's of benefit to the Chamber. Now, this gentleman says that he doesn't know anything after he left in September, so we will dispense with going through the rest of them. However, it does reflect exactly what he knew at the time and what he observed, and I will move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you talked about what you observed in the theatre, and I do believe that you said that you thought that the ARSK was woefully under-equipped. Is that basically an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I remember using words along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, on that score, sir, you were not permitted by the ARSK, or were you, to go to any of their ammunition depots?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I never went to an ammunition depot prior to the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a video, and I just want to have you look at this. And this is an HTV video, and it deals with the seizure of weaponry at Golubic. Do you know where Golubic is, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We -- so I take it you weren't aware that there was an ARSK weapons depot there?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Could you spell that location, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will put it on the screen in one second, 1D360007. This again, Your Honour, is a film HTV for the 14th of August in Golubic. Sorry. Do you know where Golubic is?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, the witness asked to spell it for him. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've never seen that spelling before. This is not my video, so I'm afraid I can't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can play it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were -- you were unaware that they had this type of weaponry. Isn't that right? And I say "they," I'm talking about the army of Republika Srpska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: What type of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The weaponry that we just saw on this video, rockets, mortars, ammunition. You were unaware that they had anything like this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I understand the take on what was seen as opposed to what was found in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that on the assumption that what was said to be found in this depot, that on the assumption that that would be accurate, that Mr. Kehoe now asks Mr. Dangerfield whether he was aware of such equipment to be available to the ARSK whether or not in Golubic. You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot comment on this specific video and this specific location. However, I did say earlier on that prior to my deployment I had training in weapons recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question, Mr. Dangerfield. In the -- in the video, whether or not accurate because you don't have any personal knowledge of that, it was explained that they found in Golubic rockets and mortars, ammunition. The question is whether you were aware that large quantities of rockets and mortars, ammunition was stored by ARSK forces. I think that, Mr. Kehoe, is the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't comment specifically on this, but I do know that armies, when they're preparing for war, have arms and ammunition dumps. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's a general statement on what armies usually do. We have to clearly distinguish from what armies usually do, what exactly there was in Golubic, but now the question was about whether you were aware of the ARSK having at its disposal in the area in which you were working large quantities of rockets and mortars, ammunition. Were you aware or were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were arms and ammunition dumps that we were told were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of this kind of heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not visits them because we were prevented from visiting them, so I could not verify specifically whether they did or did not have this level of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But they had depots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, sir, they also had -- ARSK also had tracked vehicles, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think the general description of tracked vehicles is fair, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what tracked vehicles did they have?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Specifically I can remember they had T-34 tanks, but it appeared to me that other tracked vehicles, which you could give a variety of descriptions to, had modifications to them that you would not specifically recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what tracked vehicles are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I would suggest to tracked troop carrying vehicle that might have had one or two recoilless rifles/rocket launchers welded onto the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you saw evidence of tracked vehicle movement just prior to Operation Storm, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is somewhere in one of my statements I recall reading. Could you direct me to it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I certainly can. I believe it's P698, paragraph 10. It's a -- actually, it's your report, the Brief Overview for Sector South.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Okay. Could you direct me to where?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph 10, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is reading we'll offer into evidence 1D36007, which is the video that just was played.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the statement it says: "SLO recces last week saw considerable evidence of road use by ARSK tracked vehicles."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, could we ask Madam Registrar to assign a number to the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number D715.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is a video and transcript, I take it. D715 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And where was that -- that evidence? Where did you see the evidence of the use of tracked vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I haven't got a specific location down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you don't recall?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Not the specific location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, also prior to Operation Storm, you told the Prosecutor several days ago, two days ago, that you observed the ARSK had helicopters as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: They had certainly more than one helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, how many did you see?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't recall specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also told the Prosecutor they had tanks, as you said today. How many did you see?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't recall specific numbers, but as I said earlier on, I never saw a significant gathering of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you also told the Prosecutor that you saw APCs. How many did you see?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: If I'd seen a decent sized gathering of them it would have been a memorable event. I did not see a decent sized gathering so it would not have been a memorable event. So it would not have been more than two or three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And artillery pieces, sir, did you see artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I suspect in my time there I probably saw in total throughout the area of Sector South no more than half a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, on the morning of the 4th of August, where were these APCs, the tanks, the helicopters, and the artillery pieces? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't know the specifics to that. If you can point me to it in my report, then I can give you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you do you know where all that equipment was --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- the morning of the 4th.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going back to your statement, you note in -- and I am talking about your first statement, if I may, so I can give you an accurate description of this. Paragraph 22 of -- we've got P695, your statement of 12/21/'95. Now, taking you to the days just prior to Operation Storm, and you note in paragraph 22 that there was a full mobilisation of the ARSK; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That's the information that was passed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that would --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: -- from within the headquarters of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You note in paragraph 24 of that same statement: "The ARSK stop all UN movement between Knin and UNBCP at Strmica."

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, at this particular time the battle of Grahovo had just ended and Grahovo had fallen. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I'm not aware of as to the specific date or when that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, it was in the late July period of time that Grahovo fell, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: We're looking at paragraph 25. It says: 29th of July, "Colonel Leslie tells me that the ARSK troops in the Bosanski Grahovo area are whoever they are." So that is the most detailed information I have on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you see ARSK troop and equipment movement through Knin up to Strmica in the latter part of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Sorry, could you just repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will. Using as a frame of reference your paragraph 24 on the restriction of movement between Knin and Strmica, did you see the ARSK move troops and commitment -- equipment through Knin up to Strmica in the latter part of July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think I recall seeing limited equipment. I do know there was a battle going on at some stage, because from the border crossing point at Strmica up into the mountains troops would go up, injured would come back. And when I say equipment, it might have been the odd rocket launcher, one tank. I'm sorry, I've lost the typed script on my left-hand screen. I've got two of my statements on both screens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, one of the questions that was asked about the battle of Grahovo, you said, "I'm not aware as to the specific date or when that had happened." Then Mr. Kehoe asked you, "Well, it was in the late July period of time that Grahovo fell, didn't it?" And then you answered what Colonel Leslie told you. I see in your article: "In the last week of July the Croat forces moved swiftly and decisively to take the town of Bosanska Grahovo." It surprises me a bit that where your article clearly states this that you are talking about ARSK troops in Bosanska Grahovo. The question simply was about whether it fell and that's what your article says. So therefore, I do understand that you are precise in your answers, that you do not want to say anything that you're not certain about. At the same time, you're invited to answer questions. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know in your information-gathering that the ARSK was planning a counter-attack against the HV in late July, early August of 1995? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I didn't gather that information in Sector South, so I have no idea what they were planning at the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you talking to ARSK personnel during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the information that you got came solely within UN Sector South headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, the information I got was information I gathered off the ground. So the information I gathered was specifically where I went out and gathered it for myself. There may have -- no, in fact there was information that I also gathered from the United Nations battalions within Sector South and from United Nations military observers. So I had a variety of sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, during your gathering of information from a variety of sources, did you ever hear the description of an ARSK offensive called Dinara '95?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to the 4th of August and the entire operation, and I'd like to move this into two separate areas, one the shelling, and, one the actual operation. I mean, you note in your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe -- Mr. Kehoe, I'm looking at the clock, and at the same time I get a feeling that we are moving to a bit of a different subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We, sir, we are, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd first like to have the break. But before we take a break, could I ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question may not come as a surprise. How much time you think you would need, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I look at the difficulty that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. If I look at the difficulty that I've had getting answers for this witness, I would say about three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say perhaps the difficulties might be less if you -- although I do recognise that to some extent what you say is right, to some extent also you cause part of the problem yourself by the way you're questioning the witness. The Chamber will consider also in view of the way in which you used your time until now how much time it will grant, but before we make final scheduling arrangements, and perhaps we also might delay this, but I'd like to hear from other Defence counsel how much time they would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I anticipate based on what I've heard about so far about 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Speaking from my position I could anticipate two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the existing claim -- well, at least the wishes amount to five and a half hours. Three hours for you, Mr. Kehoe, 20 minutes for Mr. Cayley, and then two and a half hours. That comes close to six hours. Perhaps as the Chamber will consider the matter, I take it that Defence counsel will consider the matter as well, I would not be surprised if the consultation with my colleagues would result in an outcome that we would certainly conclude the testimony of this witness before the recess. We have a break and we will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to deal briefly with one procedural matter. I do understand that both Prosecution and Defence would like the Chamber to -- to override the time limits under Rule 126 bis. Now, the variation of time limits under Rule 127 starts: "Save as provided by..." et cetera, et cetera, "... the Trial Chamber or Pre-Trial Chamber may on good cause being shown by motion." May I take it that your motion of all parties is that the good cause to override the time limits under Rule 126 bis is that it would cause you extreme difficulties during the recess period to respond in time. Is that your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that your motion, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber will decide on this motion in which good cause was shown for extending in general terms the time limit provided for in Rule 126 bis, that is that a response to a motion filed by a party shall be filed within 14 days of the filing of the motion, that as of next Monday, which is the first day of the recess, is extended in general terms to three weeks instead of 14 days for the two weeks to come. That means that a motion filed in the last week of the recess, that the Chamber would expect a response within 14 days. That means that you would then, within the first week after the recess -- and the recess is not four weeks, but the recess is three weeks. We are not sitting the first week after the recess. If this causes you major problems, I could extend this ruling to three weeks. It would then cover the whole of the recess but not the first week of non-sitting after the recess. What is your wish?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we contemplated that it would cover the entire four weeks. I did talk to Mr. Waespi about it, Mr. Tieger, and I think that that's what we were talking about, because I think people were otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise, then it would mean that a motion filed one day before the four weeks expire, that you would have three weeks. That sounds not, in my ears, to be the right solution. Then we would extend it to the full three weeks of the official ICTY recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that would be -- suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is the recess that starts next Monday and lasts for three weeks. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I actually perhaps didn't think through all the variations and as Mr. Kehoe indicated, I think he was communicating with Mr. Waespi on this, but I think we also contemplated that there'd be at least some measure of consideration for motions filed immediately before the recess, that somehow there'd be an extension --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to make it effective today, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today. Well, let's say on the -- is there any filing to be expected today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think that we'll probably file something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll extend that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's already filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's already filed. But of course an extension of time can be given even if the time has not yet elapsed although the motion has been filed. Then, also looking at my colleagues, but then this ruling that the 14 days time limit in Rule 126 bis, as of today, is generally extended to three weeks, and this ruling is valid for any motion filed as of today until the end of the official recess of the Tribunal, which is one week before we resume our hearings. Yes? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We have dealt with that. Then we continue with the examination of the witness. Mr. Kehoe, I looked again at Rule 90(h). You don't have to put your case to every witness. Rule 90(h) says that: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel," I think it says, "appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." So that's a very limited situation. May I draw your attention especially to both in 90(h)(i) and (ii) "...where the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party." That is the first thing to be explored and apparently there are areas where the witness is not able to do so, then of course the usual rule 90(h)(i) applies. Mr. Dangerfield, at the same time I'd like to ask you and to urge you to answer the questions in the most direct way. If you don't know, tell us. If you do know, tell it. And, Mr. Kehoe, you're invited to put questions in as direct a manner as possible to the witness. The Chamber will look at the next 55 minutes to see what would be appropriate as far as the allocation of time. I already said before, and it has not changed, that we'd like to conclude perhaps not one minute before the recess, perhaps even a bit more, because there might be a few other matters. Keep that in mind, and we'll further observe the way in which the witness is cross-examined. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, I'd like to point your attention to your brief overview report of the 4th of August. For the record that's P698. Do you have that before you, is sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go through a series of areas in this document and then ask you a few questions, and I'd like to start with paragraph 2 of that document on page 1. It notes that in the first sentence: "It was a long time before HV-HVO made any headway on the ground," and then you discuss the five areas of attack -- axes of attack, Excuse me. And if I move to -- move to paragraph 10 of this same document, and you're reflecting back on what happened on the 4th. You note that the second sentence: "G2 assessment is that Knin may fall by dark of 05 August. In order to do so, I believe that the HV will require a more successful day than today. Troops approaching from the south face a stiff opposition." And then you saw that -- that the same sentence we talked before about the tracked vehicles. And if we can go to paragraph 11: "In the west HV advances face problems of indirect major routes and at times difficult terrain in the approaches towards Knin." And once again paragraph 12: "While Knin may come under heavy artillery attack again, the considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area will require more time before they come under direct fire from HV tanks." Now, I just wanted to go through those -- those items for you. And your assessment was that, even going back to paragraph 2, is that the ground forces of the HV-HVO were having a difficult time fighting the ARSK, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: They are assessments based on the reports from the national battalions on the ground. The actual verification of the troops on the ground was not verified by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But the suffice -- I'm sorry. But it would be accurate to say, Mr. Dangerfield, that there was heavy fighting between the HV and RSK troops throughout the entire area at the commencement of Operation Storm, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The information I have given is, as I say, based on reports. I can't say for certain that there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, based on the information that you received, this is certainly what you sent down to Split and to Gornji Vakuf as to what the situation was at the end of the 4th; right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That is correct, but then I never managed to see in my entire time in Sector South sufficient forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: So my assessment was they didn't have very many forces, but the reports from the other nations suggest otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the reports from the other nations that were out in the area and observation posts, were contrary to the information that you gathered yourself. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, because they're different sources of information on different days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, if the information that you were coming back with indicated, and I'm talking about indications from the various battalions, indicated to you that there was heavy fighting between the HV and the ARSK, where did this information come from? Where did these soldiers for the ARSK come from?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The information in this particular report is based on the reports received from the outlying United Nations battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not my question, sir. My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you put two questions. The first: Where did this information come from. And then without waiting for the answer, you asked: Where did these soldiers for the ARSK come from. So these were the two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Judge. They are two questions and that was improper. And I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not easy to answer them. Of course we should explore whether the witness knew where these soldiers -- where he said he didn't know they were there where then at least they came from. Let's try to take it step-by-step. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, you noted for us that the information you were receiving from the UN battalions was that there was heavy fighting going on between the HV and the ARSK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The reports indicated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The reports that you were receiving?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: The reports at that came from the other battalions indicated that there may have been heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, my question for you is: If there were ARSK soldiers that were fighting against these HV soldiers, where did these ARSK soldiers come from?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I didn't physically see the soldiers, so I don't know where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, there was a considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: When you say "the area," could you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's go directly to your statement and maybe you can clarify it for us.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Paragraph 12: "While Knin may come under heavy artillery attack again, the considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area will require more time before they come under direct fire from HV tanks." Now, going back to the question that I asked before, and that's in line 14 when I said to you: There was a considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: See what you wrote down in this report is either not true or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that about this report at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you told your superiors in Gornji Vakuf and also in Split that there were considerable presence of forces -- of ARSK forces in the area, and by that you meant the Knin area, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's develop that further. What area did you think you were talking about, or what area were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: This is 13 years on. I believe it may have been a misuse of the English language and how it was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what you thought was going to happen, Mr. Dangerfield, was that that was going to be a bloody stand in Knin, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Could you direct me to my statement -- in my statement to the words you just used, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let's go back to paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This is your conclusion, isn't it: "The request for aid to evacuate women and children leaving behind ARSK troops shows signs of a disturbing final showdown." Now, before we move on -- excuse me let me ask a you question, sir. You believed that with the considerable ARSK resources that Knin was going to be defended in a bloody last stand, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No. I think I'm referring there to any of the civilians that were left in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's go back up to paragraph 13, and we can answer that question. "In a meeting today with UN personnel from HQ Sector South, the local RSK personnel requested humanitarian assistance. The RSK personnel were described as hysterical and in a state of bewilderment. They have asked for UN support to evacuate some 32.000 people from the Krajina, including 15.000 from the Knin area. These will be women and children up to the ages of 15. Those remaining will be purely ARSK troops." So from your own statement the evacuation was going to take place. There was, as you say in paragraph 12, a considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area, and you believed, as of the end of the day on the 4th, that this showed signs of a disturbing final showdown, or as you say two lines later in 15, "a bloody last stand." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think that would be referring to the less than a hundred soldiers I spoke about earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So when you are talking about your hundred soldiers, is that the considerable presence of ARSK forces in the area that you refer to in paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Area's not geographically specific in terms of size.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, sir, about this document. Have you met with anybody other than the Office of the Prosecutor in the past six months about your testimony in this case? And I'm not referring to members of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm talking about other people.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You haven't sat down with anybody from the British government, is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So let me ask a you question. How long were you in the military, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Sixteen years, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you're familiar with the fighting in built-up areas, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I understand that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you understand that fighting in built-up areas is probably -- I'm just waiting for the translation. And you understand that fighting in built-up areas is the bloodiest combat for an infantry soldier that there is, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And the one thing, the one thing that the military -- as a military man, the one thing you want to avoid is fighting in built-up areas because of the carnage that comes out of it. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Under certain circumstances I think that would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you are referring to this last showdown, you believed -- I'm sorry, Judge. Sorry. I apologise, Mr. Dangerfield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pause now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, when you're referring to this last showdown, this bloody last stand as you say in 15, you were referring to your belief that it would take a fight in a built-up area with a tremendous amount of carnage before Knin fell. Isn't that what you believed, and isn't that what you sent on to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I think we expected any ARSK troops that were remaining to come back to Knin. I don't think we were expecting them to go straight through Knin and out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So taking your answer, you expected retreating ARSK forces, and I take this -- by the way, let me ask you a question. What time of day did you file this report, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, as of the end of the 4th, you expected retreating -- or ARSK forces to come back into Knin for a last-pitched stand to protect the city, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That's my assessment, and that's what I would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: It's not necessarily what they would have done or what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Given the fact that you would have done it as a military man, you would agree with me it was more than reasonable for General Gotovina to conclude, as you did, that the ARSK would do the same thing, that is, have a last-pitch stand in Knin. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't know what is reasonable for General Gotovina. I don't know how he specifically operates, so I can't comment on that. Or operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the forces of the ARSK did in fact withdraw for the defence of Knin on the evening hours of the 4th, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn to you D713. This is an article or, actually, an interview from Radio Belgrade as of 2200 hours, 20 hours GMT on the 4th of August. And this is a BBC Summary Service of Radio Belgrade. If we can scroll down just a bit at mid-page. Up a little bit more. Okay. That's good. In the middle of that page, question to the -- General Mrksic: "Does this mean that they have breached the front line? "No. The disengagement line has not been changed, our forces have withdrawn to the positions to the direct defence of Knin." Do you have any information, sir, that what General Mrksic was saying is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't comment on aspects of media and journalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, isn't what General Mrksic said consistent with the report that you said -- that you wrote on the 4th of August about there going to be a final showdown and a last bloody stand? Isn't that consistent with what you wrote to your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I can't comment on General Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not asked to comment on General Mrksic. You're asked whether what you read as what General Mrksic allegedly has said, whether that would be consistent with your report. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Because I don't know that this is what General Mrksic said. This is a piece of paper with a transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dangerfield, you're not invited to -- to comment on whether these are the words of General Mrksic, yes or no. It is put to you that General Mrksic has spoken these words, and on an assumption that that is what he said, you're invited to see whether this is consistent or inconsistent with what you reported. Could you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe it is consistent, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then Mr. Kehoe intended then to have a pause, and then to ask you why. Could you explain? Mr. Dangerfield, could you explain why you consider what was put to you as the words of General Mrksic is not consistent with your report? I appreciate that you took a pause, but it was a rather long pause.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The English language is very complex, and I don't believe -- I'll just rewind. Different words and phrases mean different things, and I am not certain that what he is saying is consistent with what I am saying, and therefore I cannot say whether it is consistent or not. This is someone else's translation. It is not my translation, so it doesn't necessarily mean the same thing to me. So I am not prepared to say that it is consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you are in a position to explain to us how you understand these words. Whether that is what Mr. Mrksic meant is a totally different matter, but the wording as it comes to you now, in your understanding of the English language, which again might be a different one from mine, but could you please explain in what respect the words apparently spoken by Mr. Mrksic, as you understand them, are inconsistent with what your reporting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The paragraph begins the Mrksic paragraph, "No, the disengagement line"? Is that correct, the paragraph you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's -- that's the paragraph, sir.

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just read my bit. Okay. I believe that Mrksic is saying that his troops have withdrawn to positions and that they are controlling various areas. I refer to areas, as I'm not sure of Kordun, exactly where that is. As for "we shall create conditions," and everything else, I don't think that applies, and therefore with the advance -- with what's written in my statement, with the advancing Croatian troops looking at Knin as their final objective and ARSK troops remaining, I'm not specific on numbers. I have said: "Milan Martic will have to surrender or face a bloody last stand in the capital of Krajina," and that is my opinion. Surrender bit is not consistent with this passage of General Mrksic's, and I have -- I have written "face a bloody last stand." "A bloody last stand" does not refer to a specific number of troops and he has referred to the direct defence of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, where did you get your information about the bloody last stand and the final showdown that you put in this report?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: From the various sources within the headquarters of Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Well, it could have been the ops room, the UNMOs. Either of those sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, sir, there was still fighting -- if I can just pause a bit. There was still fighting going on on the evening of the 4th between the HV and the ARSK, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you -- read you something from a clip which is D123, 4 August, 1995, at 23.40. You remember Colonel Leslie, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I do indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Question: "In your judgement are the Croats on point of taking the town?" Talking about Knin. Leslie: "Taking Knin, no. We've had no reports of Croatians being within direct fire range of Knin, and there's still a lot of Serbs in Knin and in the surrounding hills so there we go." Was that the situation on the evening of the 4th, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: That's Colonel Leslie's interpretation of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you disagree with Colonel Leslie's interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I would disagree with "there's still a lot of Serbs in Knin."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you in Knin on the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: No, I was not, but I had been prior to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On the 5th, the fighting still continued on the 5th. And let me go to your article, and that would be The Fall of the Republic of Serb Krajina, P699, paragraph 4. This is after the -- after the carryover paragraph it is the third paragraph down on page 4. "I learnt from various sources that in the south the Croatian forces advancing from Sinj had taken considerably more ground than we expected. Intelligence revealed that they had actually advanced the full 10 kilometres. We later learned that the Croats had been counter-attacked and driven back by the Serbs twice. To the rest of the sector, the Croats had considerably less success and appeared to face much stiffer opposition." So you -- there was still a significant amount of heavy fighting between the HV and the ARSK again on the 5th of August, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Those were the reports that came in from the other battalion. They were not specifically verified, nor more importantly confirm by myself. "Heavy" is a relative term.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: But you accepted those reports, Mr. Dangerfield, and you noted that the Croats had considerably less success and appeared to face much stiffer opposition. Those were your words, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: Those were words from my interpretation of the battalion's outline. As I said, I did not specifically verify and confirm those actions, operations, ongoing battles. So then nothing was confirmed by me on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you use those reports to update your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ROLAND DANGERFIELD
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
